failure_summary.description: The instruction to retain conventional initials encouraged an unnecessary middle initial where the expected answer used the shorter unambiguous name.
Bare lists of people implicitly asked for their shared country, but the answers gave a relationship or occupational category.
The answers added a specific event qualifier or company-name suffix when the expected form was more general or shorter.
The answers returned an associated title or place instead of the requested quote completion, product, or person, despite existing target-selection rules.

patch.reasoning: Clarify that initials and other name qualifiers should be included only when needed or requested, and add a narrow rule for bare lists of people whose shared country is clearly supported. The other target-selection failures are already covered by existing rules, so they do not warrant duplicate edits.

edits.target: When choosing a name form, distinguish identity-bearing parts from generic type words supplied by the clue. Retain conventional initials that belong to a person's identifying name; omit a generic label such as an entity type or location type when the clue supplies that type and the shorter name identifies the answer unambiguously.
edits.content: When choosing a name form, distinguish the identifying name from optional initials, type or industry suffixes, and extra specificity found in a source title. Prefer the shortest common form that unambiguously answers the requested slot and matches the clue's granularity. Include a middle initial or suffix only when needed to distinguish the entity or explicitly requested; likewise, do not expand a generic term into a specific event name unless the clue asks for that specificity.

edits.target: When a prompt consists only of a list of character names or roles, use context to identify their shared work or program if that is the implied target. Return the work or program, not the performers, unless the prompt asks for the cast.
edits.content: For a bare comma- or ampersand-separated list of people, consider whether context clearly points to their shared country or jurisdiction rather than their relationship or category. If the named figures are distinctly associated with the same country, give that country; do not substitute a relationship such as “siblings” or a category such as “monarchs.” If no unique shared geographic relation is supported, do not infer one.
